results.summary: Tech-lead review of backend found no Critical prohibited-pattern violations, but there is one High-risk zero-hit upsert consistency issue plus maintainability/design alignment gaps.

findings.title: Concurrent zero-hit insert recovery continues inside a failed transaction
findings.description: The duplicate-key recovery path catches DataIntegrityViolationException from saveAndFlush and immediately queries/updates in the same @Transactional method. In JPA/Hibernate, a constraint violation during flush commonly leaves the persistence context/transaction rollback-only, so this intended concurrency fallback can still fail at commit instead of incrementing the existing zero-hit row. That undermines the core design goal that normalized keywords and DB constraints reliably prevent duplicate demand records while preserving hit counts.
findings.evidence: try { zeroHitSearchRepository.saveAndFlush(zeroHitSearch); } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException duplicate) { return zeroHitSearchRepository.findByNormalizedKeyword(normalizedKeyword).map(...).orElseThrow(...); }
findings.suggestedFix: Use a database-level PostgreSQL upsert such as INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (normalized_keyword) DO UPDATE for zero-hit recording, or move the retry to a separate transaction after the failed insert transaction has rolled back. Add a concurrency integration test that fires two same-key zero-hit records at once and asserts one row with hitCount=2.

findings.title: Case-insensitive search indexes are named as lower indexes but created on raw columns
findings.description: Product search lower-cases manufacturer, name, category, and description, and backend-design.md defines lower/case-insensitive search indexes. The migration creates idx_products_name_lower and idx_products_manufacturer_lower on raw name/manufacturer columns, so the schema name and implemented query pattern diverge. This misleads maintainers and will not support the intended lower(...) search path.
findings.evidence: CREATE INDEX idx_products_name_lower ON products (name); / CREATE INDEX idx_products_manufacturer_lower ON products (manufacturer); while ProductSpecifications uses lower(root.get(...)) for search.
findings.suggestedFix: Either create functional indexes on lower(name) and lower(manufacturer), or rename/document them as raw-column indexes. If contains search performance matters, consider a documented pg_trgm GIN strategy instead of a misleading btree index name.

findings.title: Product search/list logic exists in two repository patterns
findings.description: ProductRepository defines JPQL findInitialProducts/searchProducts methods, but production services use JpaSpecificationExecutor through ProductSpecifications instead. The JPQL methods are only exercised by repository tests, leaving two search/list implementations with different ordering and filtering behavior for maintainers to keep in sync.
findings.evidence: findInitialProducts/searchProducts are defined here; production ProductQueryService and ProductSearchService call productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable) instead.
findings.suggestedFix: Choose one pattern. Prefer deleting the unused JPQL methods and their tests if Specifications are the production path, or route services through the repository methods and remove the duplicate Specification implementation.

findings.title: Backend POM contains empty OSS publication metadata
findings.description: AGENTS.md requires OSS-publication quality and consistent license/README metadata, but backend/pom.xml contains empty url, license, developer, and SCM elements. This is not a runtime bug, but it leaves the backend module in an unfinished publication state.
findings.evidence: <url/>, <license/>, <developer/>, and SCM child elements are present but empty.
findings.suggestedFix: Select the project license, add/align the repository LICENSE, and fill Maven url/license/scm metadata. If developer identity should not be published, omit the empty developers block instead of shipping placeholder metadata.

escalations.description: Project owner must choose the OSS license and SCM metadata before backend publication metadata can be completed.

designDeviations.description: Product search indexes named idx_products_name_lower and idx_products_manufacturer_lower are implemented as raw-column indexes rather than lower/case-insensitive indexes, while production search applies lower(...) to fields.

results.summary: Architecture review of backend found no Critical layer dependency violations. findings.title: Required package convention is not implemented for model and DTO boundaries
findings.description: The architecture review standard requires `model/`, `dto/request/`, and `dto/response/` under `com.skishop`. The backend instead uses `entity/` for JPA entities and a flat `dto/` package containing both request and response records. This weakens package-level architectural signaling and makes request/response contract ownership less explicit as the API surface grows.
findings.evidence: `Product.java` declares `package com.skishop.entity;`; DTO files such as `AiConsultRequest.java` and `ProductListResponse.java` declare `package com.skishop.dto;`. Directory scan shows no `backend/src/main/java/com/skishop/model`, `dto/request`, or `dto/response`.
findings.suggestedFix: Either move JPA entities to `com.skishop.model` and split DTOs into `com.skishop.dto.request` / `com.skishop.dto.response`, or explicitly update the architecture standard to bless `entity/` and flat DTO packaging before more APIs are added.

findings.title: AiPromptBuilder is placed in service package despite being defined as a domain service
findings.description: `spec-design/backend-design.md` classifies `AiPromptBuilder` as a Domain Service, but the implementation places it under `com.skishop.service` and couples it directly to the API request DTO. Prompt construction is domain/business policy for AI consultation and should not be mixed into the application service package unless the design is intentionally revised.
findings.evidence: Line 1 declares `package com.skishop.service;`; line 3 imports `AiConsultRequest`; line 23 builds the prompt directly from that request DTO. Backend design section 2.2 lists `AiPromptBuilder` under Domain Service examples.
findings.suggestedFix: Move prompt-building policy to `com.skishop.domain` and pass a domain-oriented input/context from `AiConsultationService`, or update the design to classify prompt building as application service logic.

findings.title: Response DTO depends on persistence/entity enum
findings.description: `ZeroHitItemDto` imports `com.skishop.entity.Priority` and exposes it as part of the admin API response. Although this is not a JPA entity class leak, it couples the public API contract to the persistence/model package and makes future domain refactors observable by API consumers.
findings.evidence: Line 3 imports `com.skishop.entity.Priority`; line 17 uses `Priority priority` in the DTO record. `ZeroHitMapper` passes `zeroHitSearch.getPriority()` directly into that DTO at line 26.
findings.suggestedFix: Expose `priority` as a `String` or a DTO/API enum located under the response DTO package, and map from entity/domain priority in `ZeroHitMapper`.

findings.title: Runtime profile separation is incomplete
findings.description: The architecture standard expects common, development, and production profile separation for datasource and JPA/Hibernate settings. results.summary: DDD review found no Critical aggregate-boundary violations: repositories are per aggregate root, controllers are thin, and there are no child-entity repositories or direct JPA associations between aggregate roots. The main issues are ZeroHitSearch invariants being bypassable and key domain value concepts remaining primitive strings/BigDecimals instead of explicit Value Objects.

findings.title: ZeroHitSearch can be constructed in invalid aggregate states
findings.description: ZeroHitSearch exposes a public all-arguments constructor that assigns keyword, normalizedKeyword, hitCount, priority, opportunity loss, and timestamps without validating domain invariants such as non-blank keywords, hitCount >= 1, normalized keyword format, non-negative opportunity loss, or firstSearchedAt <= lastSearchedAt. The database has some constraints, but DDD invariants should be enforced before persistence inside the aggregate.
findings.evidence: The constructor directly assigns `this.hitCount = hitCount` and raw string fields; only null checks are applied to some fields. Invalid domain states can exist in memory until the database rejects them, if it rejects them at all.
findings.suggestedFix: Make construction go through a validating factory such as `firstHit(...)`; make the all-args constructor package-private or test-only if possible, and validate keyword/normalizedKeyword blanks, hitCount positivity, timestamp ordering, and non-negative monetary values in the aggregate.

findings.title: Zero-hit priority and opportunity-loss rules are controlled outside the aggregate
findings.description: The application service calculates nextHitCount, opportunity loss, and priority, then passes those derived values into ZeroHitSearch. ZeroHitSearch also exposes `updateDemandSignals(...)`, allowing callers to assign any priority/opportunity-loss combination. This weakens the aggregate boundary because the aggregate does not protect its own demand-signal consistency.
findings.evidence: `ZeroHitRecordingService.updateExisting` calculates `nextHitCount`, `opportunityLoss`, and `priority`, then calls `existing.recordRepeat(displayKeyword, opportunityLoss, priority, now)`. The aggregate accepts caller-supplied derived values rather than deriving or validating them itself.
findings.suggestedFix: Move repeat-recording and demand-signal recalculation behind an aggregate method such as `recordRepeat(displayKeyword, averageProductPrice, searchedAt)` or a pure domain policy invoked from inside a consistency-preserving aggregate method. Remove or restrict public arbitrary setters like `updateDemandSignals(...)`.

findings.title: Monetary and normalized keyword concepts are modeled as primitives instead of Value Objects
findings.description: The domain contains clear Value Object candidates: Product price, ZeroHitSearch estimated opportunity loss, and normalized keyword. They are represented as raw BigDecimal/String fields, so currency, scale, non-negative monetary constraints, and normalized-keyword format are not localized in immutable self-validating types as required by the DDD review standard.
findings.evidence: `Product.price` is a raw `BigDecimal`; `ZeroHitSearch.estimatedOpportunityLoss` and `normalizedKeyword` are also raw primitive-like fields in `backend/src/main/java/com/skishop/entity/ZeroHitSearch.java:30` and `backend/src/main/java/com/skishop/entity/ZeroHitSearch.java:40`. No `@Embeddable`, `@Embedded`, or domain record Value Object exists for these concepts.
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce self-validating immutable Value Objects such as `Money` and `NormalizedKeyword` and embed or convert them for JPA persistence. At minimum, centralize amount scale/currency/non-negative validation and normalized-keyword validation outside raw entity field assignment.

escalations.description: Decide whether the MVP should remain a transaction-script style CRUD/read model or raise the backend to stricter DDD tactical modeling now. The current implementation is coherent for the small scope, but it does not meet the stricter Value Object and aggregate-invariant standard.

results.summary: API endpoint review found Critical validation gaps and High REST/endpoint convention issues. URLs match the backend REST design and no legacy *.do mappings were found, but query parameters and some request fields are not protected by Bean Validation, and GET /api/products/search performs a write-side effect.

findings.title: GET product search records zero-hit state
findings.description: GET /api/products/search delegates to a service that records a zero-hit search when no products match. Because repeat calls increment demand metrics, browser retries, prefetching, crawlers, or caches can mutate server state through a safe/idempotent HTTP method.
findings.evidence: @GetMapping("/search") calls productSearchUseCase.search(...); ProductSearchService records zero-hit at lines 63-64 when totalCount == 0.
findings.suggestedFix: Keep GET /api/products/search read-only and move zero-hit recording to a POST command endpoint such as POST /api/zero-hit-searches, or explicitly document and mitigate the analytics side effect with cache-control and idempotency if the design is intentionally kept.

findings.title: Query parameters bypass Bean Validation at controller boundary
findings.description: Product and admin query parameters are accepted as raw nullable Integer/String values and passed directly to services. Some range checks occur later through IllegalArgumentException, but this does not meet the endpoint rule that all external input pass through Bean Validation, and string inputs such as q/category are not size-bounded at the API boundary.
findings.evidence: listProducts/searchProducts accept limit, category, sort, and q via @RequestParam without @Min/@Max/@Size/@Pattern and the controller has no @Validated.
findings.suggestedFix: Add @Validated to controllers and Bean Validation constraints, e.g. @Min(1) @Max(100) Integer limit, @Size(max=100) String q/category, and @Pattern for allowed sort tokens. Keep service validation as defense in depth.

findings.title: Admin zero-hit query parameters are not Bean-validated
findings.description: The admin zero-hit endpoint accepts days, sort, and limit without Bean Validation annotations before invoking the service. The service enforces ranges, but controller-level validation is skipped and sort is not constrained by @Pattern at binding time.
findings.evidence: @RequestParam days/sort/limit have no @Min/@Max/@Pattern constraints and the controller class has no @Validated.
findings.suggestedFix: Add @Validated and annotate parameters, e.g. @Min(1) @Max(365) Integer days, @Min(1) @Max(100) Integer limit, and @Pattern(regexp = "hitCount(,desc)?|lastSearchedAt(,desc)?") String sort.

findings.title: Request DTO fields are only partially constrained
findings.description: LoginRequest and AiConsultRequest use @Valid in controllers, but several fields either have no constraints or no upper bounds. This allows oversized username/password/question/keyword values and arbitrary hitCount values to reach service and prompt-building logic.
findings.evidence: AiConsultRequest.keyword, hitCount, and lastSearchedAt have no validation annotations, and question only has @NotBlank. LoginRequest line 11 has @NotBlank but no @Size bounds.
findings.suggestedFix: Add explicit constraints to all request DTO fields, e.g. @Size(max=255) username, @Size(max=200) keyword, @NotBlank @Size(max=1000) question, @Min(0) @Max(...) hitCount, and @PastOrPresent for client-supplied timestamps if accepted.

findings.title: Current-user endpoint does not use @AuthenticationPrincipal
findings.description: GET /api/auth/me reads Authentication directly and casts the principal. The endpoint-specific standard requires user-specific endpoints to bind the authenticated principal explicitly, which avoids brittle casts and makes ownership/principal use visible in the controller signature.
findings.evidence: public AuthMeResponse me(Authentication authentication) { AdminUserDto user = (AdminUserDto) authentication.getPrincipal(); ... }
findings.suggestedFix: Change the signature to public AuthMeResponse me(@AuthenticationPrincipal AdminUserDto user) and remove the manual Authentication cast.

findings.title: Global exception handler does not use ProblemDetail/RFC 9457 shape
findings.description: The handler returns a custom ApiErrorResponse rather than Spring Boot 3.2 ProblemDetail via ResponseEntityExceptionHandler. The payload is sanitized and consistent, but it does not satisfy the strict RFC 9457/ProblemDetail requirement in this endpoint review standard.
findings.evidence: @RestControllerAdvice public class GlobalExceptionHandler returns ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse>; ApiErrorResponse has timestamp/status/message/code/path/errors instead of ProblemDetail type/title/status/detail/instance.
findings.suggestedFix: Extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and return ProblemDetail for validation, auth, not-found, and unexpected exceptions, or record a project-level decision that the custom error contract is intentionally accepted.

findings.title: Admin controllers lack class-level base @RequestMapping
findings.description: AdminZeroHitController and AiConsultController put the full /api/admin/... path on methods instead of declaring a shared class-level base mapping. The endpoint behavior works, but it diverges from the controller convention requiring an appropriate class base path.
findings.evidence: AdminZeroHitController has @RestController only and @GetMapping("/api/admin/zero-hits") on the method; AiConsultController follows the same pattern with @PostMapping("/api/admin/ai-consult").
findings.suggestedFix: Add @RequestMapping("/api/admin") to each admin controller or consolidate under one admin base path, then use @GetMapping("/zero-hits") and @PostMapping("/ai-consult").

escalations.description: The provided agent definition assumes a primarily Thymeleaf MVC application, while the backend source and backend design describe a REST JSON API consumed by Next.js. This review treated the backend target as REST; maintainers should confirm that this is the intended project-level convention before enforcing @Controller/view-name rules.

The backend design allows Spring ProblemDetail or an equivalent JSON error response, while this agent standard requires ProblemDetail. Decide whether ApiErrorResponse is an accepted public contract or should be migrated to ProblemDetail.

findings.title: Concurrent zero-hit updates can lose increments
findings.description: ZeroHitRecordingService reads the existing aggregate, increments hitCount in memory, and saves the entity without optimistic locking, pessimistic row locking, or an atomic UPDATE. The duplicate-insert path handles only first-insert races; once a row exists, two concurrent searches for the same normalized keyword can both read hitCount=N, both write N+1, and lose one search. Priority and estimatedOpportunityLoss can also be calculated from stale counts.
findings.evidence: record() calls findByNormalizedKeyword(...).map(existing -> updateExisting(...)); updateExisting() computes existing.getHitCount() + 1 and saves the same entity. Repository method findByNormalizedKeyword has no @Lock and entity has no @Version.
findings.suggestedFix: Make the increment concurrency-safe: add @Version to ZeroHitSearch and retry OptimisticLockingFailureException, or use @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) for the normalized-key lookup within the transaction, or replace the read-increment-save path with an atomic @Modifying query such as UPDATE zero_hit_searches SET hit_count = hit_count + 1, last_searched_at = :now, ... WHERE normalized_keyword = :normalizedKeyword. Add a concurrent integration test that fires multiple parallel record() calls and asserts the final hitCount.

findings.title: Java 21 backend does not enable Spring Boot virtual threads
findings.description: The project targets Java 21 and Spring Boot 3.2.x, but neither the default nor Docker application configuration enables Spring Boot virtual threads. Under load, synchronous MVC, JPA, and AI-provider calls continue to consume platform request threads, which increases thread-pool exhaustion risk for I/O-heavy endpoints.
findings.evidence: application.yml defines spring.application, autoconfigure, datasource, jpa, flyway, and ai settings, but no spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true. application-docker.yml also lacks this setting.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `spring.threads.virtual.enabled: true` to the active backend configuration, then run integration tests and manually verify request logging/security behavior. Keep blocking sections out of synchronized blocks and avoid ThreadLocal-dependent application code as virtual threads are adopted.

findings.title: AI provider call blocks the request path while the service transaction remains open
findings.description: AiConsultationService is annotated @Transactional(readOnly = true), performs repository reads, then calls the AI provider synchronously before the method returns. SpringAiProviderClient uses ChatClient.prompt(...).call().content(), a blocking provider call. This can tie up a servlet request thread and may keep transaction/session resources scoped across remote I/O latency. With virtual threads disabled, slow AI calls can reduce request throughput quickly.
findings.evidence: @Transactional(readOnly = true) wraps consult(); after DB context lookup it invokes aiProviderClient.generate(prompt). SpringAiProviderClient.java:35 performs chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content().
findings.suggestedFix: Limit the read-only transaction to the database context lookup, then call the AI provider outside any transaction. Enable virtual threads for the synchronous request model, and consider enforcing provider/client timeouts so a slow provider cannot occupy request capacity indefinitely.

escalations.description: Decide whether the OSS backend should enable virtual threads globally for all profiles now, or gate it by profile after compatibility/load verification.

results.summary: Exception/logging review of backend found no empty catch blocks, System.out logging, or string-concatenated log statements. Main risks are missing request correlation via MDC, non-ProblemDetail error payloads, missing server-side stack traces for handled failures, and no production JSON log configuration.

findings.title: Requests do not get an X-Correlation-Id or MDC correlationId
findings.description: RequestLoggingFilter logs method/path/status/duration, but it never reads or generates X-Correlation-Id, never writes it to the response, never puts correlationId into MDC, and never clears MDC. A repository-wide search found no MDC or correlation ID implementation. During incidents, logs from the same request cannot be reliably joined across filters, controllers, and services.
findings.evidence: doFilterInternal only records startedAt, calls filterChain.doFilter, then logs api_request fields. No MDC.put, response.setHeader("X-Correlation-Id", ...), or cleanup is present.
findings.suggestedFix: In this filter or a dedicated OncePerRequestFilter, read X-Correlation-Id, generate a UUID when absent, set MDC.put("correlationId", correlationId), set the response header, call the chain, then remove/clear MDC in finally.

findings.title: Unexpected exception handler omits the Throwable from the server log
findings.description: The catch-all @ExceptionHandler logs only the request URI and exception class name. Because the Throwable is not passed as the final SLF4J argument, the stack trace and root cause are lost from server logs while the client receives a sanitized 500. This makes production root-cause analysis unnecessarily slow.
findings.evidence: LOGGER.error("Unexpected API error at {} with type {}", request.getRequestURI(), exception.getClass().getName());
findings.suggestedFix: Use `LOGGER.error("Unexpected API error at {}", request.getRequestURI(), exception);` or include any safe structured fields while keeping the Throwable as the final argument.

findings.title: AI provider fallback catch block drops exception details from logs
findings.description: AiConsultationService catches AiProviderException and returns a controlled fallback response, but the warning log records only providerStatus=ERROR. The wrapped provider failure and stack trace are not logged, so transient provider failures cannot be diagnosed from logs.
findings.evidence: catch (AiProviderException exception) { ... LOGGER.warn("ai_consultation providerStatus={}", response.providerStatus()); }
findings.suggestedFix: Log the exception as the final SLF4J argument without logging the prompt or API key, for example `LOGGER.warn("ai_consultation providerStatus={}", response.providerStatus(), exception);`.

findings.title: Global errors use custom ApiErrorResponse instead of Spring ProblemDetail
findings.description: The global handler returns ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse> for validation, authentication, not-found, invalid-parameter, and unexpected errors. The review standard requires Spring Boot ProblemDetail/RFC 7807-style responses from @ControllerAdvice. This is a deliberate frontend-friendly contract, but from this review perspective it deviates from the required error model.
findings.evidence: public ResponseEntity<ApiErrorResponse> handleValidation(...) and build(...) creates new ApiErrorResponse(...).
findings.suggestedFix: Return `ProblemDetail` from exception handlers, set stable fields such as `code`, `path`, and validation `errors` via `setProperty`, and update frontend contracts/tests if the API contract changes.

findings.title: Production JSON/logstash logging is not configured
findings.description: The backend has spring-boot-starter-actuator, but no logstash-logback-encoder dependency and no logback-spring.xml. Without JSON logs containing app name, level, timestamp, correlationId, and trace fields, log aggregation and structured querying will be weaker in production.
findings.evidence: Dependencies include actuator, JPA, security, validation, web, Flyway, Spring AI, H2, PostgreSQL, and test dependencies; no `net.logstash.logback:logstash-logback-encoder`. No logback file was found under backend/src/main/resources.
findings.suggestedFix: Add `logstash-logback-encoder` and a `logback-spring.xml` JSON appender that includes `spring.application.name`, `%X{correlationId}`, and trace/span IDs when tracing is enabled.

findings.title: User-supplied search keywords are written to application logs
findings.description: Zero-hit recording logs normalizedKeyword. The value originates from a user search keyword and can contain accidental PII such as an email address, phone number, or address even if the intended domain is product search. This is not proof of current PII leakage, but it is a logging data-minimization risk.
findings.evidence: LOGGER.info("zero_hit_recorded normalizedKeyword={} hitCount={} priority={}", saved.getNormalizedKeyword(), ...); repeated again on insert at lines 92-96.
findings.suggestedFix: Avoid logging raw keywords. Log a zero-hit row id, a stable hash, keyword length, hitCount, and priority; keep the actual keyword in the database where access is governed by application controls.

findings.title: Actuator metrics are not exposed or instrumented for operations
findings.description: Actuator is present, but management endpoint exposure is limited to health. results.summary: Data-access review found one critical configuration issue and several high-impact JPA convention/concurrency gaps in backend. No files were modified.

findings.title: Datasource URLs have hardcoded fallbacks in default runtime configuration
findings.description: The default application configuration falls back to concrete PostgreSQL JDBC URLs when SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL is unset. Per the data-access standard, runtime connection strings should come from environment variables or explicit local/dev profiles, so production cannot silently boot against an unintended database.
findings.evidence: url: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL:jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/skishop}
findings.suggestedFix: Make SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL required in default/prod config, and move localhost or Docker defaults to an explicitly activated local/dev profile or sample env file. Apply the same policy to application-docker.yml if it is used outside local demos.

findings.title: Entity primary keys use UUID and entity-level generation instead of String UUID generated in the service layer
findings.description: Both JPA entities declare UUID primary keys, and Product also generates IDs in @PrePersist while ZeroHitSearch generates IDs in the entity factory/@PrePersist. The review standard requires a String UUID primary key with UUID.randomUUID().toString() generated in the service layer and no persistence-layer generation.
findings.evidence: @Id / @Column(nullable = false, updatable = false) / private UUID id;
findings.suggestedFix: Change IDs to String with @Column(name = "id", length = 36, nullable = false, updatable = false), remove @PrePersist ID generation, generate UUID strings in the service/factory boundary, and update migrations/tests consistently.

findings.title: Column names are not explicitly declared for all entity fields
findings.description: The entities rely on implicit column naming for several fields. The data-access standard requires every persisted field to declare @Column(name = "snake_case") explicitly, including columns whose Java field name currently matches the database column name.
findings.evidence: Examples include @Column(nullable = false, updatable = false) on id, @Column(nullable = false, length = 100) on manufacturer, and @Column(nullable = false) on name without name attributes.
findings.suggestedFix: Add explicit name attributes to all @Column annotations, for example @Column(name = "manufacturer", nullable = false, length = 100), and do the same in ZeroHitSearch for id, keyword, and priority.

findings.title: Zero-hit repeat recording can lose increments under concurrent searches
findings.description: ZeroHitSearch is a mutable aggregate with hitCount increments, but it has no @Version column and the update path performs read-modify-save. Concurrent requests for the same normalized keyword can both read the same hitCount and persist the same incremented value, losing one search event. Insert races are retried via unique constraint handling, but repeat-update races are not protected.
findings.evidence: int nextHitCount = existing.getHitCount() + 1; ... existing.recordRepeat(...); ZeroHitSearch saved = zeroHitSearchRepository.save(existing);
findings.suggestedFix: Add @Version Long version to ZeroHitSearch plus a Flyway migration, handle ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException/OptimisticLockException with retry or a business exception, or replace the repeat path with an atomic UPDATE ... hit_count = hit_count + 1 query.

findings.title: Product audit timestamps are maintained manually instead of Hibernate audit annotations
findings.description: Product.createdAt and Product.updatedAt are audit timestamps, but they are populated via @PrePersist/@PreUpdate and Instant.now(). The standard requires @CreationTimestamp and @UpdateTimestamp for audit timestamps, which keeps audit behavior centralized in Hibernate and avoids accidental drift from manual lifecycle code.
findings.evidence: createdAt/updatedAt are plain @Column fields, with values assigned in prePersist() and preUpdate().
findings.suggestedFix: Annotate createdAt with @CreationTimestamp and @Column(name = "created_at", nullable = false, updatable = false); annotate updatedAt with @UpdateTimestamp and @Column(name = "updated_at", nullable = false). results.summary: Static security review of backend found Critical issues in secret handling and brute-force protection, plus High-risk gaps around public state mutation, security headers, request limiting, bearer-token lifecycle, and user-input logging. findings.title: Docker profile ships a hardcoded database password fallback
findings.description: The docker profile uses a literal fallback password (`skishop`) for `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD`. If the profile is deployed without overriding the environment variable, the application uses a predictable database credential. This violates the repository standard that secrets in yml/properties must be environment-only placeholders.
findings.evidence: password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD:skishop}
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the literal fallback: `password: ${SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD}`. Put non-secret sample values in `.env.example`, and make docker/compose startup fail fast when the password is absent.

findings.category: A07 Identification and Authentication Failures / Rate Limiting
findings.title: Admin login has no rate limiting or account lockout
findings.description: `/api/auth/login` is explicitly public, and `AdminAuthService.login` performs a direct credential check with no failed-attempt counter, lockout duration, throttling, IP/user rate limit, or retry delay. An attacker can perform credential stuffing or brute-force attempts against the single admin account.
findings.evidence: SecurityConfig permits POST /api/auth/login at line 63; login() checks username/password and immediately throws on mismatch with no throttling or lockout state.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a rate-limiting filter for `/api/auth/login` and failed-attempt tracking keyed by username and source IP. Lock the account or block the source after a small threshold, return a unified authentication failure, and emit structured security events without logging credentials.

findings.category: STRIDE Tampering / CSRF Semantics / Business Logic Abuse
findings.title: Public GET search endpoint mutates zero-hit analytics state
findings.description: `GET /api/products/search` is public, but a zero-result search records or updates `zero_hit_searches`. Because this is a state-changing side effect on a safe HTTP method, any external page or bot can trigger drive-by GET requests and poison demand analytics without authentication or CSRF protection.
findings.evidence: SecurityConfig permits GET /api/products/search at line 62. ProductController exposes it as GET at lines 43-49. ProductSearchService records zero-hit rows when `totalCount == 0`.
findings.suggestedFix: Make product search GET read-only. Move analytics recording to a deliberate POST endpoint protected by CSRF or anti-abuse controls, or keep server-side recording but add strict rate limiting, bot controls, and safeguards so cross-site GETs cannot pollute the table.

findings.category: Security Headers / XSS Defense in Depth
findings.title: CSP, Referrer-Policy, Permissions-Policy, and explicit HSTS policy are not configured
findings.description: The security filter chain does not configure a headers policy. Spring Security provides some defaults, but the required defense-in-depth headers in the review standard, especially `Content-Security-Policy`, `Referrer-Policy`, and `Permissions-Policy`, are absent from source configuration. Missing CSP materially weakens containment if any frontend or API-rendered content path becomes XSS-prone.
findings.evidence: The HttpSecurity chain configures csrf/cors/session/auth/exception handling but has no `.headers(...)` block. `rg` found no CSP/referrer/permissions header configuration in backend/src/main.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an explicit `.headers(...)` block with `contentSecurityPolicy`, `referrerPolicy`, `permissionsPolicy`, `frameOptions`, `contentTypeOptions`, and HSTS settings appropriate for the deployment TLS model. Also add integration tests asserting the headers.

findings.title: Request body and free-text inputs are not bounded
findings.description: The backend has no configured request-size limits, and free-text fields such as product search `q`, AI `keyword`, and AI `question` lack `@Size` constraints. Public search uses the raw keyword in multiple LIKE predicates and may attempt to persist it into `VARCHAR(255)`, while admin AI consultation can send arbitrarily large prompts to the provider. This creates DB, memory, thread, and external-cost DoS paths.
findings.evidence: The server section only configures error disclosure. `AiConsultRequest` lines 10-14 has `@NotBlank` only on `question`; ProductController accepts `String q` at line 45 with no size validation.
findings.suggestedFix: Configure HTTP limits such as Tomcat post/header/swallow sizes and JSON body limits where applicable. Add Bean Validation constraints such as `@Size(max = 100)` for search keywords and bounded `@Size` for AI questions, and reject overlong values before repository or provider calls.

findings.title: Bearer tokens cannot be revoked and repeated logins create unlimited active tokens
findings.description: Logout is disabled and the in-memory session map only removes expired tokens when those tokens are later presented. Successful repeated logins create additional valid bearer tokens with an 8-hour default TTL. A stolen token remains usable until expiry, and login floods can grow token state unbounded.
findings.evidence: `logout(AbstractHttpConfigurer::disable)` disables logout. AdminAuthService issues tokens with default `PT8H` TTL and stores them in `sessions.put(...)` at lines 95-100, with no revoke/logout method or per-user session cap.
findings.suggestedFix: Add logout/revoke support, cap active tokens per admin, invalidate older tokens on new login or password/config rotation, periodically purge expired sessions, and reduce TTL or use refresh-token rotation if longer sessions are required.

findings.title: User-controlled search keywords are logged without redaction
findings.description: Zero-hit recording logs `normalizedKeyword`, which is derived from public user search input. Search terms can contain email addresses, tokens, names, or other sensitive data accidentally pasted by users. This creates a PII leakage path into application logs.
findings.evidence: LOGGER.info("zero_hit_recorded normalizedKeyword={} ...", saved.getNormalizedKeyword(), ...) logs the normalized user search keyword. The same pattern appears on insert at lines 92-95.
findings.suggestedFix: Do not log raw or normalized user search terms. Log a stable hash, length, category of event, hit count, and priority, or redact values with an allowlist/PII detector before logging.

findings.category: Business Logic Attack Resistance / Race Condition
findings.title: Zero-hit aggregate updates are vulnerable to lost updates
findings.description: For existing zero-hit keywords, the service reads the row, increments `hitCount` in memory, and saves it without optimistic or pessimistic locking. Concurrent requests for the same keyword can overwrite each other, causing inaccurate demand counts and priority calculations. This is especially relevant because public search can trigger the update path.
findings.evidence: `findByNormalizedKeyword(...).map(existing -> updateExisting(...))`; `updateExisting` computes `existing.getHitCount() + 1` and saves. The `ZeroHitSearch` entity has no `@Version`, and the repository method has no lock annotation.
findings.suggestedFix: Add an `@Version` column to `ZeroHitSearch` and retry/handle `OptimisticLockingFailureException`, or use a repository-level atomic update/pessimistic lock for hit-count increments.

escalations.description: Decide whether the docker profile is intended for local-only demos or any deployable environment. If deployable, the hardcoded DB password fallback must be removed before OSS publication.

Confirm the authentication architecture: the review standard assumes session-management controls, while the implementation uses stateless bearer tokens. The chosen model needs an explicit threat model for token storage, revocation, TTL, and XSS exposure.

designDeviations.description: The implementation uses stateless opaque bearer tokens instead of the session-based model assumed by the security review checklist. Session cookie controls are not applicable, but equivalent token lifecycle controls are currently incomplete.

findings.title: All test methods violate the required should_ExpectedResult_when_Condition naming pattern
findings.description: The backend test suite uses descriptive camelCase method names, but none of the @Test methods follow the mandated should_ExpectedResult_when_Condition pattern. The scan found 64 @Test methods and 0 methods matching should_*_when_*. This makes test names less specification-like under the supplied review standard.
findings.evidence: Examples: keywordNormalizerTrimsLowercasesAndCollapsesWhitespace(), opportunityLossCalculatorUsesHitCountTimesAverageProductPrice(), priorityDeciderUsesMvpHitCountThresholds(). Similar naming appears across controller, service, repository, entity, and application tests.

findings.title: Some tests combine multiple Act operations and multiple behaviors in one test method
findings.description: Several tests bundle multiple method calls or scenarios into a single test. This violates the requested Act singularity rule and makes failures harder to diagnose.
findings.evidence: validLoginIssuesDistinctTokenAndValidatesAdminUser() calls login twice and validateToken in the same test. loginFailsWhenCredentialsAreMissingWrongOrUnconfigured() executes six independent failing login scenarios in one method.
findings.suggestedFix: Split into focused tests or parameterized tests, each with one Act block. Example: should_issueDistinctTokens_when_validCredentials(), should_validateAdminUser_when_tokenIsKnown(), should_throwAuthenticationFailed_when_usernameIsMissing(), should_throwAuthenticationFailed_when_passwordIsWrong().

findings.description: The existing JaCoCo report shows overall branch coverage at 83%, but several important classes are below the 80% branch threshold expected for services and public behavior. These gaps include provider availability/error branches and zero-hit query validation branches.

findings.title: No tests use @DisplayName for human-readable specifications

results.summary: Performance review found no N+1 relationship risks, but several High issues remain around limit-only pagination, duplicate count queries, and entity fetching on public list/search paths.

findings.title: Collection APIs implement only first-page limiting, not retrievable pagination
findings.description: Product and zero-hit list paths normalize requests to PageRequest.of(0, limit, ...), so clients can only retrieve the first page/top-N rows. Product responses include totalCount, but no page/size metadata; zero-hit responses include neither explicit page nor size metadata. Under production-sized datasets this prevents real paginated traversal and conflicts with the performance review requirement for Pageable/Page-style collection APIs with metadata.
findings.evidence: return PageRequest.of(0, safeLimit, toSort(sort));
findings.suggestedFix: Add a validated page or offset parameter to the controllers/use cases, construct PageRequest.of(page, size, sort), and return pagination metadata such as page, size, totalElements, and totalPages. Apply the same pattern to /api/admin/zero-hits instead of hard-coding page 0.

findings.title: Product listing can execute the same count query twice
findings.description: JpaSpecificationExecutor.findAll(specification, pageable) returns a Page and commonly executes a count query for full pages. The service discards the Page and then calls productRepository.count(specification), adding an unnecessary second count round trip on the public listing path.
findings.evidence:
List<Product> products = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable).getContent();
long totalCount = productRepository.count(specification);
findings.suggestedFix: Keep the Page<Product>: Page<Product> page = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable); then map page.getContent() and use page.getTotalElements(). If total counts are not required, return a Slice to avoid count queries entirely.

findings.title: Product search duplicates the pageable count query and uses it for zero-hit logic
findings.description: The search path uses findAll(specification, pageable).getContent() and then count(specification). Like the listing path, Spring Data can already execute a count for the Page, so the explicit count creates duplicate work on a high-traffic endpoint. The same total can be reused for zero-hit detection.
findings.evidence:
List<Product> products = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable).getContent();
long totalCount = productRepository.count(specification);
findings.suggestedFix: Use Page<Product> page = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable); long totalCount = page.getTotalElements(); and base zero-hit recording on that value. Consider Slice plus a cheap exists/count path only if the API no longer needs exact totals.

findings.title: Public product list/search fetch managed Product entities instead of DTO projections
findings.description: The public product APIs fetch Product entities, then map them to ProductDto in memory. ProductDto currently mirrors most product columns, so the column waste is limited, but this still allocates managed JPA entities and incurs persistence-context overhead on a hot read path. Interface/class DTO projections would reduce entity materialization cost and make selected columns explicit.
findings.evidence:
List<Product> products = productRepository.findAll(specification, pageable).getContent();
return new ProductListResponse(products.stream().map(productMapper::toDto).toList(), totalCount);
findings.suggestedFix: Introduce repository projection methods returning ProductDto or ProductSummary projections for list/search queries, or use Criteria/JPQL constructor projections. Keep entity loading only for update flows or domain behavior that needs managed entities.

findings.title: Search predicate is index-unfriendly and likely scans products as data grows
findings.description: Product search applies lower(...) and leading-wildcard LIKE against manufacturer, name, category, and description. The migration creates plain B-tree indexes on raw columns, which do not help this pattern, especially with '%keyword%'. This is database-side evaluation, but it will degrade toward table scans for larger catalogs.
findings.evidence:
String pattern = "%" + keyword.trim().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) + "%";
criteriaBuilder.like(criteriaBuilder.lower(root.get("manufacturer")), pattern), ...
findings.suggestedFix: For PostgreSQL, use pg_trgm GIN indexes or full-text search for contains matching, and align migrations with the actual predicate. If prefix-only search is acceptable, avoid the leading wildcard and add expression indexes for lower(column).

findings.title: AI consultation reloads product master context on every request
findings.description: The consultation service queries distinct categories and manufacturers for every AI consult request. Product categories/manufacturers are seeded master-like data and are unlikely to change frequently, so this repeats low-cardinality reads without a cache strategy.
findings.suggestedFix: Cache the prompt context or each distinct lookup with Spring Cache. If future admin product updates are added, evict the cache on product create/update/delete.

findings.title: Zero-hit summary scans the same time window three times
findings.description: ZeroHitQueryService builds summary metrics with three separate repository aggregate calls over the same since predicate. This adds round trips and repeated index/range scans for each admin radar request.
findings.evidence:
new ZeroHitSummaryDto(
		zeroHitSearchRepository.countRadarItems(since),
		zeroHitSearchRepository.sumHitCount(since),
		zeroHitSearchRepository.sumEstimatedOpportunityLoss(since));
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the three aggregate methods with one projection query returning count, sum(hitCount), and sum(estimatedOpportunityLoss) in a single database round trip.

findings.title: Prompt list formatting creates an intermediate list and concatenates strings in reduce
findings.description: AiPromptBuilder.formatList collects a stream to a list, re-streams it, then concatenates strings in reduce. The method caps at 20 items, so the impact is bounded, but the pattern creates avoidable allocations and repeated String copies.
findings.evidence:
values.stream()...
		.toList()
		.stream()
		.reduce((left, right) -> left + System.lineSeparator() + right)
findings.suggestedFix: Use Collectors.joining(System.lineSeparator()) directly after mapping, or String.join on the capped stream result. This removes the second stream and repeated concatenation.

escalations.description: Decide whether the public API contract should remain top-N only for the current demo or be upgraded to true page/size pagination. The performance standard requires true pagination, but frontend contract tests currently assert a limit/totalCount shape.

findings.title: Live AI provider call is not protected by retry or circuit breaker
findings.description: `SpringAiProviderClient.generate` performs the live Spring AI call directly. The project has no Resilience4j dependency/configuration and the call path has no `@Retry`, `@CircuitBreaker`, or equivalent Spring Retry protection. A transient AI provider outage will immediately degrade every live request instead of being retried with bounded backoff and isolated by an open circuit.
findings.evidence: `String answer = chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content();` is called inside a plain try/catch. `backend/pom.xml` contains no Resilience4j/Spring Retry dependency and `backend/src/main/resources/application.yml` contains no `resilience4j` section.
findings.suggestedFix: Add Resilience4j Spring Boot 3 support, then annotate the provider boundary, for example `@Retry(name = "aiProvider", fallbackMethod = "fallback")` and `@CircuitBreaker(name = "aiProvider", fallbackMethod = "fallback")`. Configure `maxAttempts: 3`, exponential backoff, failure threshold, and open-state duration in `application.yml`. Keep fallback returning the existing controlled fallback/error response path.

findings.title: AI provider client has no explicit timeout contract
findings.description: The Spring AI/OpenAI client is constructed with API key and model only. No connect/read/response timeout is configured in code or application properties, so a slow provider or network stall can hold the admin request thread until library or network defaults decide to fail.
findings.evidence: `OpenAiApi.builder().apiKey(aiProperties.apiKey()).build()` and `OpenAiChatModel.builder()...build()` do not set timeout values. `application.yml` only defines `app.ai.api-key` and `app.ai.model`.
findings.suggestedFix: Externalize an AI timeout property such as `app.ai.response-timeout: PT30S` and apply it through the Spring AI/OpenAI builder API or a configured Spring HTTP client/request factory with connect and response timeouts.

findings.title: AI provider calls have no concurrency isolation
findings.description: The live AI call runs on the request path without `@Bulkhead`, rate limiter, or another concurrency cap. If the provider slows down, concurrent admin AI consultations can consume servlet request capacity and amplify the timeout issue.
findings.evidence: The external call is made directly via `chatClient.prompt(prompt).call().content()` and repository search found no `@Bulkhead`, `@RateLimiter`, or bulkhead configuration in `backend/src/main`.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a semaphore bulkhead around the AI provider boundary, for example `@Bulkhead(name = "aiProvider", type = Bulkhead.Type.SEMAPHORE)`, and configure a small `maxConcurrentCalls` appropriate for admin traffic and provider quota.

findings.title: No non-blocking health signal exists for the AI provider
findings.description: Actuator health and probe support are enabled, and this matches the design goal that AI provider health should not block base readiness. However, there is no custom health indicator or health contributor for the AI provider, so operators cannot distinguish core app health from live AI provider degradation via health/observability endpoints.
findings.evidence: Health exposure and probes are configured, but source search found no `HealthIndicator`, `ReactiveHealthIndicator`, or custom AI provider health contributor under `backend/src/main/java`.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a lightweight, non-readiness-blocking `HealthIndicator` or metric for the AI provider status. Keep it out of readiness if the AI feature is optional, consistent with `backend-design.md`, but expose enough authorized detail for operations.

findings.title: Graceful shutdown is not configured
findings.description: The backend does not configure graceful shutdown or shutdown phase timeout. During deploys or container termination, in-flight requests, including slow AI consultations, can be interrupted instead of being drained predictably.
findings.evidence: The `server` section configures only error response detail settings. There is no `server.shutdown: graceful` and no `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` in `application.yml` or `application-docker.yml`.
findings.suggestedFix: Configure `server.shutdown: graceful` and a bounded `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase`, for example `20s`, then ensure container/Kubernetes termination grace periods are at least as long.

escalations.description: Decide whether retrying AI consultations is acceptable from a cost and duplicate-token-usage perspective. If yes, keep retries low and limited to transient network/provider exceptions.
Decide whether AI provider health should remain auxiliary only or be included in a separate authorized health group. The current backend design says AI health should not block base readiness.
